prompt: Bonus depreciation generally allows eligible businesses to:

options.text: Deduct qualifying property cost in the year placed in service up to a taxable income limit
Deduct a large percentage of qualifying property cost in the year placed in service
Deduct a large percentage of real property cost, including buildings, in the first year
Take a first-year deduction only for new property not previously used by anyone

explanation: Bonus depreciation interacts with §179 and regular MACRS; eligibility depends on property type and placed-in-service date.

distractorExplanations.a: The taxable-income limit applies to §179 expensing; bonus depreciation can create or increase a loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Buildings (27.5/39-year property) do not qualify; bonus applies to property with a recovery period of 20 years or less.
distractorExplanations.d: Since TCJA, used property acquired from unrelated parties also qualifies for bonus depreciation.

prompt: A small business using the cash method of accounting generally recognizes income when:

options.text: An invoice is mailed regardless of payment
The fiscal year ends on June 30 by IRS mandate
Payment is actually or constructively received
Accrual entries are required for all inventory businesses without exception

explanation: Cash method timing differs from accrual; certain taxpayers must use accrual (e.g., some inventory-heavy businesses).

distractorExplanations.a: Unpaid invoices may not be income under cash method.
distractorExplanations.b: June 30 year-end is not mandatory for all businesses.
distractorExplanations.d: Inventory rules can force accrual for some taxpayers.

prompt: For payments made in tax year 2025, Form 1099-NEC is generally used to report:

options.text: Payments of $600 or more for rent and prizes paid by a business
Payment card and third-party network transactions above the reporting threshold
Nonemployee compensation of $5,000 or more paid to a corporation
Nonemployee compensation of $600 or more paid in the course of a trade or business

explanation: For 2025 payments, Form 1099-NEC reports nonemployee compensation of $600 or more paid in a trade or business, such as fees to independent contractors. Legislation enacted in 2025 raises this threshold for payments made after 2025, so check the form year's instructions.

distractorExplanations.a: Rents, prizes, and awards are reported on Form 1099-MISC; Form 1099-NEC is for nonemployee compensation.
distractorExplanations.b: Card and payment-app transactions are reported by settlement entities on Form 1099-K, not Form 1099-NEC.
distractorExplanations.c: Payments to corporations are generally exempt from 1099-NEC (attorney fees excepted), and $5,000 is not the threshold.

prompt: An employer generally needs an Employer Identification Number (EIN) to:

options.text: Identify the business on tax returns, payroll deposits, and information returns
Report employee wages on Form W-2 in place of each employee's Social Security number
Obtain the electronic filing identification number required to e-file returns
Replace the owner's SSN on the owner's own Form 1040

explanation: EIN is the business federal tax ID; employees still use SSNs on W-2s.

distractorExplanations.b: Form W-2 shows the employer's EIN and each employee's SSN; the EIN does not replace employee SSNs.
distractorExplanations.c: An EFIN comes from the IRS e-file provider application; an EIN is the business taxpayer ID.
distractorExplanations.d: An EIN identifies the business; the owner still uses an SSN on the individual Form 1040.

prompt: The accumulated earnings tax for corporations generally targets:

options.text: Personal holding companies earning mostly passive investment income such as dividends and royalties
Corporations accumulating earnings beyond reasonable business needs to avoid shareholder-level tax
S corporations with accumulated E&P from C years and excess passive investment income
C corporations paying dividends beyond current earnings and profits to their shareholders

explanation: AET is a C corporation penalty tax concept; reasonable needs of the business is a key defense.

distractorExplanations.a: Passive-income companies face the separate personal holding company tax and are excluded from the accumulated earnings tax.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the §1375 tax on S corporations' excess passive income, not the accumulated earnings tax.
distractorExplanations.d: Distributions exceeding E&P are a return of capital; AET penalizes retaining, not distributing, earnings.

prompt: Losses on sales between related parties are generally:

options.text: Deductible currently if the sale price equals fair market value as set by an appraisal
Deferred until the related buyer resells, then deducted by the original seller at that time
Disallowed currently, with potential offsetting rules when the related party later sells
Disallowed currently and added to the related buyer's basis

explanation: Related-party loss disallowance prevents shifting losses; basis and holding period rules also apply.

distractorExplanations.a: §267 disallows losses between related parties even when the price equals appraised fair market value.
distractorExplanations.b: The original seller does not get the loss later; the buyer may use it to reduce gain on a later resale.
distractorExplanations.d: The disallowed loss is not added to the buyer's basis; it can be used to offset the buyer's later gain.

prompt: Uniform capitalization (UNICAP) rules may require businesses to:

options.text: Expense direct and indirect production costs as period costs
Capitalize all selling and marketing costs into inventory
Capitalize certain indirect costs into inventory or produced property
Capitalize indirect costs even if gross receipts are under $31 million

explanation: UNICAP affects manufacturers, resellers, and producers by requiring capitalization of allocable costs.

distractorExplanations.a: UNICAP requires capitalizing allocable direct and indirect costs, not expensing them as period costs.
distractorExplanations.b: Selling, advertising, and distribution costs are excluded from UNICAP; it covers production and resale costs.
distractorExplanations.d: Small businesses meeting the §448(c) gross receipts test ($31 million for 2025) are exempt from UNICAP.

prompt: A business bad debt is generally deductible as:

options.text: A short-term capital loss when the debt becomes totally worthless
An ordinary loss using the reserve method for estimated bad debts
An ordinary loss for unpaid cash-basis fees not yet reported as income
An ordinary loss when worthlessness or partial charge-off is established

explanation: Nonbusiness bad debts are typically short-term capital losses; business bad debts follow different treatment.

distractorExplanations.a: Short-term capital loss treatment applies to nonbusiness bad debts; business bad debts are ordinary losses.
distractorExplanations.b: The reserve method is not allowed for most taxpayers; business bad debts use the specific charge-off method.
distractorExplanations.c: Cash-method taxpayers cannot deduct uncollected fees not included in income; there is no basis in the receivable.

prompt: When a C corporation has a net operating loss, current law generally:

options.text: Limits NOL deductions to a percentage of taxable income in carryforward years
Allows a two-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward with no percentage limit
Limits NOL carryforwards to 80% of taxable income for 20 years before expiration
Allows a five-year carryback for losses arising in any tax year

explanation: Post-TCJA NOL rules include an 80% taxable income limitation for many carryforwards and restricted carrybacks.

distractorExplanations.b: That is pre-TCJA law; post-2017 NOLs carry forward indefinitely and are capped at 80% of taxable income.
distractorExplanations.c: The 80% cap is right, but post-2017 NOLs carry forward indefinitely rather than expiring after 20 years.
distractorExplanations.d: The five-year carryback was a temporary CARES Act rule for 2018–2020 losses, not current law.

prompt: Reasonable compensation for an S corporation shareholder-employee is scrutinized because:

options.text: Distributions above basis are subject to SE tax for active owners
IRS can recharacterize distributions as wages if salary is set too low
High wages reduce the corporate AAA and trigger built-in gains tax
Wages must equal at least 60% of S corporation net income

explanation: When an S corporation pays a shareholder-employee unreasonably low wages and takes the rest as distributions, the IRS can recharacterize those distributions as wages and assess FICA and employment taxes; reasonable compensation is judged on the services performed.

distractorExplanations.a: Distributions above basis are capital gain, not SE income; the concern is distributions recharacterized as wages.
distractorExplanations.c: Wages are deductible and do not trigger §1374 built-in gains tax; AAA is reduced by distributions and losses.
distractorExplanations.d: No fixed 60% rule exists; reasonable compensation is a facts-and-circumstances test of services rendered.

prompt: Start-up costs for a new business are generally:

options.text: Capitalized and amortized over 60 months
Capitalized and depreciated over 39 years
Capitalized and amortized over 180 months
Deducted in full up to $50,000 in year one

explanation: Organizational and start-up costs have specific capitalization and §195 amortization rules. Up to $5,000 can be expensed immediately (phased out above $50,000), with the rest amortized.

distractorExplanations.a: Sixty months was the pre-2004 §195 amortization period; current law uses 180 months.
distractorExplanations.b: 39 years is the nonresidential real property life; start-up costs are amortized over 180 months.
distractorExplanations.d: $50,000 is the phase-out threshold; the immediate deduction is $5,000, reduced dollar-for-dollar above it.

prompt: Controlled group rules for related employers primarily affect:

options.text: Sharing of graduated corporate tax brackets among members of the controlled group
Consolidated filing of one Form 1120 for brother-sister groups
Treatment of each member's employees as independent contractors
Combined employee counts and benefit plan discrimination testing limits

explanation: Controlled groups must aggregate employees for retirement plan coverage and nondiscrimination testing.

distractorExplanations.a: Graduated corporate brackets ended with the flat 21% rate under TCJA, so bracket sharing no longer matters.
distractorExplanations.b: Consolidated returns are for affiliated parent-subsidiary groups; brother-sister groups cannot file one return.
distractorExplanations.c: Worker classification uses common-law control tests; controlled group status does not convert employees.

prompt: Transfer pricing documentation for related-party cross-border transactions generally must show:

options.text: Prices and terms are consistent with arm's-length dealings between unrelated parties
Prices match the related parties' cost plus a fixed 10% markup
Prices and terms follow the parent company's internal budget rates approved by its board
Prices and terms minimize combined worldwide tax for the group

explanation: IRS and OECD guidelines require contemporaneous documentation supporting arm's-length pricing for international related-party deals.

distractorExplanations.b: Cost plus is one possible method, but no fixed 10% markup is required; results must fall in an arm's-length range.
distractorExplanations.c: Internal budget rates are not a §482 standard; pricing must reflect what unrelated parties would agree to.
distractorExplanations.d: Minimizing worldwide tax is not a §482 standard; the IRS may reallocate income that departs from arm's length.

prompt: Section 199A Qualified Business Income deduction limitations may reduce the benefit when:

options.text: Adjusted gross income exceeds thresholds and the business has no W-2 employees
Taxable income exceeds thresholds and the business is a specified service trade or business
Taxable income is below thresholds and the business pays no W-2 wages
The business is an S corporation paying its shareholder-employee reasonable compensation

explanation: W-2 wage and UBIA limits phase in above thresholds; SSTBs face additional restrictions.

distractorExplanations.a: Limits key off taxable income before the QBI deduction, not AGI; wage limits matter above the threshold.
distractorExplanations.c: Below the threshold the W-2 wage and UBIA limits do not apply, so the full 20% deduction is generally available.
distractorExplanations.d: S corporation income qualifies; the owner's reasonable compensation is excluded from QBI but causes no limitation.

prompt: When representing a client in an IRS examination, the practitioner should generally:

options.text: Sign the original return on the taxpayer's behalf once a Form 2848 is filed
Answer only the IRS correspondence sent to the representative, leaving taxpayer notices aside
Bring a second client's records to show the agent consistent industry practice
Review the power of attorney, understand the scope, and communicate through authorized channels

explanation: Representation requires valid authority (e.g., Form 2848) and adherence to Circular 230 duties.

distractorExplanations.a: A Form 2848 does not authorize signing a return unless the narrow Reg. 1.6012-1(a)(5) conditions are met and stated.
distractorExplanations.b: Notices sent to the taxpayer also need a response; representatives coordinate replies to relevant IRS correspondence.
distractorExplanations.c: Sharing another client's records breaches §7216 and Circular 230 confidentiality duties.

prompt: To petition the U.S. Tax Court after receiving a statutory notice of deficiency, the taxpayer generally must file within:

options.text: 90 days from the date the notice was mailed
120 days from the date the notice was mailed
150 days from the date the notice was mailed to a U.S. address
180 days from the date the notice was mailed

explanation: The 90-day period is jurisdictional; missing it forecloses Tax Court review of the deficiency. Requests to pay or extensions of time to pay do not extend the period; it is 150 days if the notice is addressed outside the U.S.

distractorExplanations.b: No 120-day rule applies; the petition is due within 90 days (150 days if addressed outside the U.S.).
distractorExplanations.c: 150 days applies when the notice is addressed to a person outside the U.S.; U.S. addresses get 90 days.
distractorExplanations.d: 180 days is not a Tax Court deadline; the deficiency petition is due 90 days after the notice is mailed.

prompt: Form 433-A or 433-B is commonly used in collection cases to:

options.text: Authorize a representative to receive confidential collection information from the IRS
Provide financial information for installment agreements, OIC, or CNC determinations
Request a Collection Due Process hearing after a final notice of levy
Compute the trust fund recovery penalty for responsible business officers

explanation: Collection financial statements document income, expenses, assets, and liabilities for IRS collection decisions.

distractorExplanations.a: Information authorization uses Form 8821 (or 2848); Forms 433-A/B are collection financial statements.
distractorExplanations.c: CDP hearings are requested on Form 12153; Form 433-A/B supplies financial data within collection cases.
distractorExplanations.d: TFRP is proposed via Letter 1153 after a Form 4180 interview; Form 433-B describes a business's finances.

prompt: A substitute for return (SFR) filed by the IRS generally means:

options.text: The IRS accepted a return the taxpayer filed after the extended due date
The IRS filed a return for the taxpayer that includes all available deductions
The IRS prepared a return from information documents when the taxpayer failed to file
The IRS converted a joint return to MFS after a spouse disputed it

explanation: SFRs often omit beneficial deductions; filing a true return may be preferable when allowed.

distractorExplanations.a: A late original return filed by the taxpayer is still a taxpayer return; an SFR is prepared by the IRS for nonfilers.
distractorExplanations.b: SFRs typically use single or MFS status and the standard deduction, omitting deductions and credits the taxpayer could claim.
distractorExplanations.d: SFR has nothing to do with MFS conversions; it is an IRS-prepared basis for assessing a missing return.

prompt: An installment agreement request for an individual balance due generally:

options.text: Stops interest from accruing once the agreement is approved
Requires Form 433-A for every balance, even under $10,000
Reduces the balance owed to what the taxpayer can afford
Allows monthly payments when the IRS approves terms

explanation: Installment agreements accrue interest and may include user fees; larger balances may need detailed financials. Terms depend on the amount owed and the taxpayer's financial ability.

distractorExplanations.a: Interest continues to accrue on the unpaid balance under an installment agreement; only the failure-to-pay rate drops.
distractorExplanations.b: Guaranteed and streamlined agreements under $50,000 generally need no Form 433-A financial statement.
distractorExplanations.c: Reducing the amount owed is an Offer in Compromise; an installment agreement spreads payment of the full balance.

prompt: The Collection Statute Expiration Date (CSED) generally marks:

options.text: The end of the IRS period to collect assessed tax unless extended by certain events
The end of the IRS period to assess additional tax after the return is filed
The last day to claim a refund of an overpayment for the tax year
The date an installment agreement must be fully paid to avoid default

explanation: CSED is typically ten years from assessment, extended by OIC, bankruptcy, CDP, or other events.

distractorExplanations.b: Assessment generally must occur within 3 years (ASED); the CSED is the 10-year collection period after assessment.
distractorExplanations.c: Refund claims follow the 3-year/2-year rule of §6511; the CSED governs IRS collection, not refunds.
distractorExplanations.d: IA terms may run to the CSED, but the CSED itself is the statutory end of the collection period.

prompt: Currently Not Collectible (CNC) status generally means:

options.text: The IRS writes off the balance after six months
The IRS pauses enforced collection
The taxpayer stops filing returns while in hardship
Penalties and interest stop accruing on the balance

explanation: CNC is temporary hardship relief; liabilities remain and interest may continue. CNC applies when the taxpayer cannot pay basic living expenses.

distractorExplanations.a: CNC does not forgive the debt; the balance remains on the account and the CSED keeps running.
distractorExplanations.c: Taxpayers in CNC must continue filing returns; noncompliance can end CNC status.
distractorExplanations.d: Interest and the failure-to-pay penalty generally continue to accrue during CNC status.

prompt: The Trust Fund Recovery Penalty (TFRP) may be assessed against responsible persons for:

options.text: Negligent failure to deposit the employer's share of FICA
Willful failure to pay the corporation's income tax balance
Willful failure to collect or pay over withheld employment taxes
Willful failure to file Forms W-2 with the SSA on time

explanation: TFRP targets withheld income and FICA taxes considered held in trust for the government.

distractorExplanations.a: TFRP covers withheld trust fund taxes (income tax and employee FICA) and requires willfulness, not negligence.
distractorExplanations.b: Corporate income tax is not a trust fund tax; TFRP applies to withheld employment taxes.
distractorExplanations.d: Late W-2 filing triggers information-return penalties under §6721, not the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty.

prompt: The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) generally:

options.text: Processes PTIN applications and renewals for paid return preparers
Administers the Special Enrollment Examination for EA candidates
Reviews disputed audit adjustments as an independent appeals forum
Investigates practitioner misconduct and may impose sanctions

explanation: OPR handles Circular 230 discipline; tax law administration is separate IRS functions.

distractorExplanations.a: PTINs are administered by the IRS Return Preparer Office; OPR handles Circular 230 discipline.
distractorExplanations.b: The SEE is run by the IRS through its testing vendor, not by OPR, whose role is disciplinary.
distractorExplanations.c: Independent review of audit disputes is the IRS Independent Office of Appeals, not OPR.

prompt: The Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) primarily helps taxpayers who:

options.text: Face economic harm or have unresolved IRS problems
Want an independent review of an audit adjustment
Need free return preparation through VITA sites
Seek a private letter ruling on a proposed transaction

explanation: TAS is an independent organization within the IRS focused on systemic and hardship cases. TAS steps in when normal IRS channels cannot fix the problem timely.

distractorExplanations.b: Independent review of audit adjustments is the Office of Appeals; TAS resolves hardship and systemic problems.
distractorExplanations.c: VITA and TCE provide free preparation; TAS helps with unresolved IRS problems and economic harm.
distractorExplanations.d: PLRs are issued by IRS Chief Counsel; TAS does not rule on substantive tax law questions.

prompt: A jeopardy assessment may be made when the IRS believes:

options.text: The taxpayer filed a frivolous return position
Collection of tax is in jeopardy
The assessment statute will expire within 90 days
The taxpayer has missed two installment payments

explanation: Jeopardy assessments are extraordinary immediate assessments with limited prior notice. Typical triggers: the taxpayer may quickly leave the country or dissipate assets.

distractorExplanations.a: Frivolous returns draw the §6702 $5,000 penalty; jeopardy assessments are about collection being endangered.
distractorExplanations.c: An expiring statute calls for a statute extension or quick assessment; jeopardy depends on collection risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Missed IA payments lead to default notices and possible levy, not a jeopardy assessment.

prompt: The general refund claim statute for an overpayment is often:

options.text: Two years from the return filing date or three years from the date the tax was paid
Three years from the date of assessment, or ten years if unpaid
Three years from the return due date (or filing date) or two years from payment
Ten years from the date of assessment, matching the CSED period

explanation: Refund statutes differ from assessment statutes; missed deadlines can forfeit refunds.

distractorExplanations.a: The periods are reversed: three years from filing or two years from payment, whichever is later.
distractorExplanations.b: The assessment date and the 10-year collection statute do not set the refund claim period under §6511.
distractorExplanations.d: Ten years is the collection statute; refund claims follow the 3-year/2-year rule of §6511.

prompt: IRS certification of seriously delinquent tax debt may lead to:

options.text: Suspension of the taxpayer's state driver's license by the IRS
A 15% FPLP levy on Social Security benefits
Denial of a U.S. visa for the taxpayer's foreign spouse
State Department denial or revocation of a U.S. passport

explanation: Fixing Debt Passport law links large unpaid debts to passport actions after certification procedures.

distractorExplanations.a: Federal tax debt certification affects passports; driver's license suspension is a state child-support or state tax tool.
distractorExplanations.b: The Federal Payment Levy Program is a separate collection tool; §7345 certification goes to the State Department.
distractorExplanations.c: Certification affects the delinquent taxpayer's own passport, not visas for relatives.

prompt: When the IRS issues a summons to a taxpayer or third party, the recipient generally:

options.text: May comply, challenge in court within time limits, or seek to quash
Must comply within 10 days or face arrest without a court order
May petition the Tax Court within 90 days to quash the summons
May ignore it unless the IRS re-serves it through state court

explanation: Summons enforcement goes through district court; privileges and relevance may be litigated.

distractorExplanations.b: IRS summonses are enforced through a federal district court; there is no self-executing arrest power.
distractorExplanations.c: Third-party summons challenges go to federal district court (20-day petition to quash), not the Tax Court.
distractorExplanations.d: State courts play no role; IRS summonses are enforced in federal district court under §§7402 and 7604.

prompt: A Kovel arrangement (accountant working with attorney) generally:

options.text: Extends attorney-client privilege to an accountant's return preparation work once an attorney engages the firm
May extend attorney-client privilege to an accountant hired by counsel to help the attorney provide legal advice
Gives the accountant the §7525 federally authorized practitioner privilege in criminal tax investigations
Lets the accountant represent the client before Appeals without filing a Form 2848 for the periods

explanation: Kovel covers accountants engaged to assist counsel with legal advice; ordinary compliance work remains unprivileged. It does not cover routine return preparation.

distractorExplanations.a: Return preparation is not legal advice, so Kovel privilege does not cover it even when counsel hires the accountant.
distractorExplanations.c: The §7525 privilege does not apply in criminal matters, and Kovel rests on attorney-client privilege, not §7525.
distractorExplanations.d: Kovel engagements concern privilege; representation before the IRS still requires a valid Form 2848.

prompt: Enrolled Agents must generally complete continuing education including:

options.text: No continuing education after initial SEE passage
Ethics hours and federal tax law updates over a three-year enrollment cycle
Ethics training once per lifetime
Only state real estate courses with no tax content

explanation: EA CE requirements are published by IRS; failure can affect enrollment status.

distractorExplanations.a: CE is ongoing, not one-time.
distractorExplanations.c: Ethics is recurring, not lifetime-only.
distractorExplanations.d: Real estate CE does not substitute for EA tax CE.

prompt: Form 8867 (Paid Preparer's Due Diligence Checklist) is required when claiming:

options.text: Credits such as the premium tax credit and dependent care credit on paid returns
Credits such as EITC, CTC, and the Lifetime Learning Credit on any return
Certain credits such as EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, and AOTC on paid-prepared returns
The EITC only, when the client has no qualifying children

explanation: Due diligence includes knowledge questions, document retention, and credit eligibility verification.

distractorExplanations.a: Form 8867 covers EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, and HOH status, not the premium tax credit or dependent care credit.
distractorExplanations.b: The Lifetime Learning Credit is not covered by Form 8867, and the form applies to paid-prepared returns.
distractorExplanations.d: Form 8867 covers the EITC with or without children plus CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, and HOH filing status.

prompt: Paid preparers who file more than the IRS threshold of individual returns generally must:

options.text: E-file those returns only if clients sign Form 8948 consents
Register for an EFIN, then paper-file returns over the limit
E-file those returns once they file 100 or more per year
E-file those returns unless an approved hardship exception applies

explanation: E-file mandates promote accuracy and processing efficiency; exceptions are limited.

distractorExplanations.a: Form 8948 documents a client's choice to paper file; the default for specified preparers is e-file.
distractorExplanations.b: An EFIN lets a preparer e-file; it does not permit paper-filing returns that fall under the e-file mandate.
distractorExplanations.c: The specified tax return preparer threshold is 11 or more individual or trust returns per year, not 100.

prompt: A paid tax return preparer must generally:

options.text: Sign the return and provide the firm's EIN instead of a PTIN
Sign the return only if they hold an EA, CPA, or attorney credential
Sign the return and provide an identification number (PTIN) on the return
Provide the PTIN but leave signing to the taxpayer alone

explanation: Preparer signature and PTIN identify who prepared the return for IRS enforcement.

distractorExplanations.a: The firm EIN may also appear, but each signing preparer must enter a personal PTIN on the return.
distractorExplanations.b: Paid preparers must sign whether credentialed or not; credentials do not determine the signing duty.
distractorExplanations.d: Both the taxpayer and the paid preparer sign; the preparer's signature requirement is separate under §6695(b).

prompt: When an e-filed return is rejected for an invalid or mismatched taxpayer identification number, the preparer should:

options.text: Contact the client, verify the correct TIN, and retransmit after correction
Retransmit with the mismatched dependent removed, without asking the client first
Use an ITIN from the client's prior file to force acceptance
Paper-file the same return to avoid the e-file TIN match

explanation: E-file rejects must be resolved with accurate data; fabricating TINs is fraud.

distractorExplanations.b: Changing a return without the client's knowledge is improper; the client must confirm data and approve changes.
distractorExplanations.c: Substituting an old ITIN without verification risks a false return; the correct current TIN must be confirmed.
distractorExplanations.d: Paper filing with a wrong TIN still fails processing; the TIN must be verified and corrected first.

prompt: IRC §7216 restricts:

options.text: IRS employees' disclosure of return information to state tax agencies and others
Disclosure or use of tax return information without client consent or an exception
Disclosure of return information by the taxpayer to a mortgage lender
Preparer advertising that guarantees refunds or IRS approval

explanation: §7216 governs preparers and others handling return data; marketing uses often need consent.

distractorExplanations.a: IRS disclosures are governed by §6103; §7216 applies to return preparers and related persons.
distractorExplanations.c: Taxpayers may share their own information freely; §7216 restricts preparers and others in the tax business.
distractorExplanations.d: Misleading advertising falls under Circular 230 §10.30, not the §7216 return-information rules.

prompt: A 'ghost preparer' who prepares returns but does not sign or use a PTIN:

options.text: Is permitted if the client signs and files the return as self-prepared with no preparer
Is permitted for preparers who file fewer than 11 returns a year
Violates preparer rules and exposes clients to errors and identity theft risk
Shifts the §6694 penalties for the return onto the client

explanation: Ghost preparers evade oversight; clients should verify PTIN and signature on returns.

distractorExplanations.a: A client's signature does not cure the paid preparer's duty to sign and enter a PTIN under §6695.
distractorExplanations.b: Eleven returns is the e-file mandate threshold; every paid preparer must still sign and use a PTIN.
distractorExplanations.d: §6694 penalties are preparer penalties; clients face accuracy penalties for their own understatements.

prompt: For an undisclosed return position, the §6694(a) unreasonable-position standard is generally met if the position lacks:

options.text: More-likely-than-not support
A realistic possibility of success
Substantial authority
A supporting opinion of counsel

explanation: Undisclosed positions need substantial authority; disclosed positions may rely on reasonable basis. Tax shelters use a more-likely-than-not standard.

distractorExplanations.a: More-likely-than-not applies to tax shelters and reportable transactions; ordinary undisclosed positions need substantial authority.
distractorExplanations.b: The one-in-three realistic possibility standard was replaced in 2007; undisclosed positions now need substantial authority.
distractorExplanations.d: No opinion of counsel is required; the §6694(a) test turns on whether substantial authority supports the position.

prompt: When advising on a tax return position, a practitioner should consider:

options.text: Whether the position is likely to be audited, since low audit risk supports taking it
Whether the client is willing to pay the preparer penalty if assessed
The refund amount and whether disclosure would trigger an examination
The strength of authority supporting the position and whether disclosure is prudent

explanation: Circular 230 and §6694 frameworks emphasize reasonable inquiry and supportable positions.

distractorExplanations.a: §10.37 and §6694 analysis may not weigh audit risk; positions are judged on their merits and authority.
distractorExplanations.b: Preparer penalties fall on the preparer and cannot be shifted by client agreement; authority strength controls.
distractorExplanations.c: Refund size and fear of examination are not proper factors; disclosure decisions turn on the level of authority.

prompt: If a practitioner discovers a material error on a prior-year client return they prepared, Circular 230 generally expects:

options.text: Prompt advice to the client about the error and consequences of non-correction
Filing an amended return for the client before the statute closes
Notifying the IRS of the error if the client refuses to file an amended return
Withdrawing from all future work for the client immediately

explanation: Practitioners should advise correction paths; they cannot force amendments but must not ignore known material errors.

distractorExplanations.b: Under §10.21 the practitioner advises the client; amending requires the client's decision and signature.
distractorExplanations.c: Circular 230 does not require reporting the client to the IRS; the duty is to advise and consider withdrawal.
distractorExplanations.d: Withdrawal is not required; §10.21 requires advising the client, and later conduct may affect future work.

prompt: Refund anticipation loan (RAL) arrangements advertised to clients should:

options.text: Describe the loan as an IRS expedited refund once e-filed
Clearly disclose fees, that the loan is from a lender (not the IRS)
Disclose the loan fees only after the client signs the lender's loan documents
Present the refund transfer fee as an IRS processing charge

explanation: Transparent RAL disclosures prevent misleading borrowers about timing and costs. Disclosures should also note that the actual refund may differ from the loan amount.

distractorExplanations.a: RALs are third-party loans; describing them as IRS refunds is misleading under Circular 230 §10.30.
distractorExplanations.c: Fees must be disclosed before the client commits; post-signing disclosure defeats informed consent.
distractorExplanations.d: The IRS charges no e-file processing fee; refund transfer and loan fees belong to the bank or preparer.

prompt: When a client is identity theft victim, a practitioner should generally advise:

options.text: Filing Form 8821 so the IRS can lock the client's account
Filing Form 8857 to have the fraudulent return removed from the client's account
Filing Form 14039 or following IRS Identity Theft Victim Assistance procedures
Filing a paper return with a new SSN requested from the IRS

explanation: IP PINs, identity theft affidavits, and specialized IRS units help resolve account issues.

distractorExplanations.a: Form 8821 is an information authorization; identity theft victims file Form 14039 and may get an IP PIN.
distractorExplanations.b: Form 8857 requests innocent spouse relief; identity theft affidavits use Form 14039.
distractorExplanations.d: The SSA, not the IRS, issues SSNs and rarely changes them; the IRS protects victims with IP PINs.

prompt: Circular 230 standards for written tax advice generally require a practitioner to:

options.text: Follow the former covered-opinion rules for any advice on listed transactions
Rely on a promoter's representations about the facts if the practitioner discloses that reliance
Include a disclaimer that the advice cannot be used to avoid penalties
Base the advice on reasonable factual and legal assumptions and consider relevant authorities

explanation: After withdrawal of the old covered-opinion rules, Circular 230 §10.37 sets a single written-advice standard of reasonable assumptions and due diligence.

distractorExplanations.a: Covered-opinion rules (§10.35) were withdrawn in 2014; §10.37 now applies one standard to written advice.
distractorExplanations.b: Reliance on a promoter is unreasonable under §10.37 when the advisor knows or should know of the conflict.
distractorExplanations.c: The Circular 230 penalty disclaimer became unnecessary after the 2014 amendments; it is not required.

prompt: When relying on client-provided records, a practitioner under Circular 230 should:

options.text: Make reasonable inquiries when facts appear incomplete or inconsistent
Accept any statement without question to speed filing
Fabricate supporting documents if the client forgot them
Ignore red flags because the client bears all preparer penalties alone

explanation: Reasonable reliance is allowed with due diligence; willful blindness violates professional standards.

distractorExplanations.b: Blind acceptance fails due diligence.
distractorExplanations.c: Fabricating documents is unlawful.
distractorExplanations.d: Preparers share penalty exposure under §6694 and Circular 230.

prompt: Best practice for retaining client tax workpapers generally includes:

options.text: Keeping records for one year and shredding client originals after e-filing
Keeping records for the required period and returning client-owned documents on request
Keeping client originals until fees are paid and discarding workpapers after filing
Keeping only the signed Form 8879 and returning all other documents to clients

explanation: Retention supports due diligence defense; clients own their underlying documents.

distractorExplanations.a: Preparers must keep return copies or a list for 3 years; client originals should be returned, not shredded.
distractorExplanations.c: §10.28 requires returning client records even in fee disputes, and workpapers support due diligence.
distractorExplanations.d: Form 8879 must be kept 3 years, but due diligence also requires retaining supporting records and workpapers.
